utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic, the Chamber was informed that there was a matter you'd like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. There is only one short matter I would like to raise this morning before the witness is with us. We have a deadline to provide evidence D44 and we are trying to get it from Radio TV of Serbia, who was allegedly in charge of that, actually they produced it, but we haven't received any response from this institution so if we can get some additional time. I was informed last night but my -- actually two nights ago by my investigators that they have not been able to acquire this video yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, any objection against some additional time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, just to not forget about it, it would be good that we give ample extra time, let's say, four, six weeks, so that we don't lose -- that we don't forget about it. So then you'll have to provide that evidence -- well, let's say by the 10th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other matter? If not, then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I'd like to make a corrigendum on behalf of the Chamber to the 12th, 92 bis decision which was filed yesterday. In the disposition under 6, Witness RM308 under (a), the second line says transcript pages 5588, line 16, to 5518, line 18, and that should be 5588, line 16, to page 5588, line 18. To the extent that was not yet clear because one usually reads forwards and not backwards, it's hereby put on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milovanovic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that is that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic will now cross-examine you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're ready, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Milovanovic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will start from some very general points that you are very familiar with. I'm going to ask you about the role of UNPROFOR and NATO in the developments in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Would you agree with me if I say that UNPROFOR was in charge of the situation in the territories under its control?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was Satish Nambiar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just already for the first question, to be in charge of the situation, does that mean that you have to provide the weather forecast or does that mean that you have to provide food to the population, or that you have to keep an eye on the armament? I mean, it's a -- even with yes as an answer, it doesn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I have been reprimanded after the first question. I hope that we will not continue in that way. When we said that UNPROFOR was responsible for the situation in the territories under its control, what does that imply?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the four mandates of UNPROFOR in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was exactly what you are talking about. When it comes to the control of the situation on the ground, UNPROFOR effectively mediated and it was supposed to do it objectively, between the warring parties. UNPROFOR was supposed to organise negotiations, help the warring parties achieve agreements on various things, and the basic mandate of UNPROFOR was to safely conduct UNPROFOR convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you about Satish Nambiar. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in the theatre of war, Satish Nambiar, who was an Indian general, was the UNPROFOR commander for the entire territory of the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when this gentleman left? Why did he leave, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a well-known fact that Satish Nambiar resigned before his mandate was over. I don't know how long his term of office was supposed to be. In my conversation with General Mladic, I learned that Nambiar had left because he had learned that reports by his subordinates, the commander of UNPROFOR for Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, reached the Supreme Command of NATO before they reached the Security Council. I believe that that was the main reason why he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what was the relationship between UNPROFOR and NATO? How did things change over time, if they did?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, that relationship changed. At first, UNPROFOR had the mandate that I described, and it seemed to me that it did function independently and honoured its mandates. However, yesterday I mentioned a date, the 16th and 17th December 1992, when a decision was made by the highest officers of NATO and the Western European union, and I quote from that decision, according to which Republika Srpska would be subject to bombardment if it didn't meet some of the demands by the Security Council or international institutions. That plan was given under the authority of the command of UNPROFOR; i.e., the UNPROFOR commander for Bosnia-Herzegovina had the right to decide whether he would seek NATO intervention or not. That was interference; i.e., the mandate of UNPROFOR was extended beyond the resolution of the Security Council. NATO launched its activities on the 11th of April, 1994. It was just a threat, but we were first bombarded in Gorazde, but then that practice continued. Whenever we failed to meet a requirement we would be given an ultimatum and it was NATO that bombarded us, not UNPROFOR, not the local UNPROFOR that was deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, we knew that all officers and generals who worked for UNPROFOR were actually members of NATO. They came from NATO. They were affiliated with NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you perceive NATO as a neutral side in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From the 17th December 1992 onwards I perceived NATO alliance as an enemy, as I already told you yesterday. It was the fourth enemy that Republika Srpska had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question to the witness? In your previous answer you said, Mr. Milovanovic, "... all officers and generals who worked for UNPROFOR were actually members of NATO." What about the Ukrainian company in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there may have been exceptions, you know. However, all the generals hailed from NATO members. I knew that there was a Ukrainian battalion which was later joined by Russians, but those countries voluntarily joined efforts in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I don't think that there were any high-ranking officers among them. When I said "all," you are free to alter it into a majority, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, when did you become aware of the plan for the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina according to the principle 51 per cent in favour of the Federation of Croats and Muslims, and 49 per cent for Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- the announcement of such a division of Bosnia-Herzegovina first appeared in the press, in Belgrade. I also heard a statement of the then-president of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic. I heard that there were negotiations about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when that was, if you can remember? Was it at the end of 1993 or perhaps the beginning of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was towards the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now I'm going to ask you something about the protected areas. As a matter of fact, I read your statements and while reading them I discovered something that I didn't know before, although I had been involved in these trials for a long time. There were only two protected areas, Srebrenica and Zepa, which resulted from an agreement between the Serbian and Muslim sides with the mediation of UNPROFOR; whereas all the other protected areas were imposed and did not involve the warring parties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Lukic, you are using a wrong term. You're using the material "protected areas." No agreement was ever reached about protected areas because this is an entirely different category based on the Geneva Conventions. We should be talking about secure areas and the difference is huge. A protected area is an area which must not be attacked by any side, and the third power guarantees that; whereas safe areas is based on an agreement to stop combat in a certain area, and it is true that negotiations with General Morillon started already on the 29th of January. I'm not sure of the date. You shouldn't hold me to it. I heard of that safe areas for the first time when the vice Prime Minister used it, Nikola Koljevic. He told me that the areas of Srebrenica and Zepa should be neutralised because according to General Philippe Morillon, about 64.000 refugees found shelter in Srebrenica. Among the 64.000 refugees, there were about 12.500 armed men. As for Zepa, which is a small settlement in Eastern Bosnia, Morillon told me that about 32.000 refugees were sheltered there. First he mentioned the figure of 38.000 and then he corrected himself and said 32.000. Koljevic asked me whether it should be good for these two places to be blocked and demilitarised, and that armed forces should be excluded from that -- from those two areas so that the civilian population could live peacefully. The UNHCR would provide food and all the other bare necessities to the civilian population. And let me tell you this: That was the conversation between the two of us, but I liked the idea because I thought if the armed forces - I mean the Muslim armed forces - were excluded from those areas, that would free our armed forces that had to hold the areas in encirclement. Finally on the 8th of May, General Mladic and General Sefer Halilovic, under the patronage or under the supervision, if you will, of General Philippe Morillon signed an agreement on the demilitarisation of Srebrenica. A few days later, or more precisely, on the 18th of May, the same agreement was signed for the area of Zepa. As for Gorazde --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, could you refer to the year in which it happened? Second, if you take a breath now and then, the interpreters can take a breath now and then as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. The year for Srebrenica and Zepa was 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was actually the reason for my intervention. We didn't have the year and for the record, years are very important. How many protected areas -- or I apologise, how many safe areas were eventually established in Bosnia-Herzegovina apart from Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a total of six safe areas. For two of them, agreements were signed. They were Srebrenica and Zepa. The Security Council unilaterally proclaimed the following safe areas: Tuzla, Sarajevo, Gorazde, Bihac. The sixth is missing, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I said Sarajevo. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was also the sixth safe area for which an agreement was signed, and this is the area of Mount Igman and Bijelasnica, and that happened in the second half of August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will come to that. In any case, there were those four and the two for which the agreement was signed, so six in total; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an agreement for Gorazde as well but it was signed a year later, in the second half of April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Following the signing of the agreement which made Srebrenica a safe area, a certain number of civilians and wounded were evacuated from Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall how many civilians were evacuated on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the agreement on the safe area of Srebrenica was signed, an agreement was reached with General Philippe Morillon, sometime in late February, whereby the ill and the wounded would be evacuated from Srebrenica, as well as a number of civilians who wished to be evacuated. The Army of Republika Srpska took upon itself to create a corridor from Srebrenica to Bratunac to Caparde and on to Tuzla to enable the people to leave the area. In return, Morillon was to make sure that the Serbs in Tuzla who wanted to leave that town would be enabled to do so. By happenstance, it was I who was placed in charge of engaging in these negotiations with General Morillon, in the presence of General Zdravko Tolimir and I don't know who else, perhaps Rajko Balac was there from the Main Staff. I alerted the attention of General Morillon to the fact that this would be ethnic cleansing regardless of the fact that the United Nations would be involved in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The simple question was how many civilians were evacuated. You give us the full story of the evacuation and we are about to hear what the weather conditions were, but the question was how many civilians were evacuated. Could you please answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 12.500 civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Nevertheless, I will ask you to continue giving your answer because you have anticipated a great many questions that I was to put to you. Did the Serbs leave Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single Serb left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What became of those Serbs in Tuzla who didn't leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They stayed behind in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you know, if you discussed the issue with anyone, the fact that the Serbs stayed in Tuzla, was it of their own free will? What happened or what became of the Serbs in Tuzla after the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked General Morillon why was it that he aborted the evacuation of civilians from Srebrenica and why did the Serbs stay behind in Tuzla? His answer was that the Serbs refused to leave Tuzla because they would remain to protect their properties. Now, as for the question why the evacuation of the people from Srebrenica was aborted, he had no answer to give to me, although I divined it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the conclusion you reached as for the fact that the evacuation of civilians from Tuzla was discontinued?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among the 12.500, Morillon allowed the majority of the members of the so-called Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to leave Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it seems that there is confusion. The witness told us that 12 and a half thousand civilians left, were evacuated. Then you asked about the evacuation of Serbs from Tuzla. Your last question was about the evacuation of civilians from Tuzla and what was the reason that it was discontinued. And then it seems that from the answer that the witness refers to the evacuation of persons from Srebrenica. And he again mentions the 12.500 which we heard earlier in relation to the evacuation of civilians from Srebrenica. So there seems to be a miscommunication. Could you please seek to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that you clarified and summarised it well. And the witness would agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we would like to have an answer to the question. The question was: What caused the evacuation of civilians, in your view, to be discontinued from Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no evacuation in Tuzla to speak of, not a single Serb was pulled out, so you can't really speak of something having been discontinued if it hasn't begun in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What caused them not to move out from Tuzla? And I do understand that you did not agree with the explanation given by General Morillon. What is your explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my thinking, not an explanation. I don't think that Morillon ever gave the opportunity to the Serbs in Tuzla to leave the town. Out of 17.500 Serbs who were present in Tuzla at the time, it is quite an impossibility that not a single one would agree to leave the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am a little confused, Mr. Milovanovic. I think a little earlier you assert that Serbs in Tuzla did not want to leave because they wanted to protect their properties. Now, when you now say General Morillon did not give them that opportunity, I wonder whether they didn't know at all that they had the option to leave, if they were not given the opportunity, or were they given the opportunity but they did not want to leave because they wanted to protect their property.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I said that not a single Serb left Tuzla. I asked General Morillon what the reason for this was, and this is his explanation, i.e. that they refused to do so because they preferred to stay behind in Tuzla to protect their properties. That was Morillon's explanation. Now, my thinking was that they had not even been offered the possibility to leave Tuzla because, I repeat, it is quite impossible that out of 17.000 Serbs in Tuzla, not a single one would agree to leave the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And they wanted -- did they want to leave? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I had to accept General Morillon's explanation that they refused to leave Tuzla. I was not able to verify that -- if that was indeed true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, in the course of your work, did you ever come by information to the effect that the Serbs were killed in minefields in an attempt to leave Tuzla or that they paid money to be able to get out of Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not come by such information because the general area of Tuzla was not within my sphere of interest. What was within my sphere of interest was the theatres of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm moving to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be asking you now about the other protected areas or, rather, safe areas, I apologise. General Mladic keeps correcting me. I keep making the mistake over and over again. Let's talk about Bihac because I think that it's an area that you're most familiar with. Is it true that there were three brigades in Bihac which was also declared a safe area, and I mean three brigades of the Muslim 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the information we received from the BH command of UNPROFOR, that the 5th Corps had the three brigades and that all the three brigades were disarmed under Article 60 of Protocol I, Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the information sent out by UNPROFOR correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, or, rather, later on, it would become apparent that it was not true. Just as in Srebrenica and Zepa, where agreements were signed making those towns a safe area, we wanted to make the same agreements in respect of Bihac. However, it was the Security Council which unilaterally declared it a safe zone, and as an interested party we were there simply to receive information from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, what happened on the 23rd of October, 1994, in relation to Bihac?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd of October, 1994, the commander of the 5th Corps of the so-called Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, General Atif Dudakovic, came out of the safe area of Bihac, across the Una River, launched an attack against the VRS-controlled areas at the foot of the Grmec Mount. He attacks radially from Bihac downstream the Una, in the direction of Kulen Vakuf. Prior to that, that same 5th Corps defeated the forces of -- well, I shouldn't call him rogue, really, but an independent unit of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he left Izetbegovic's army, that is to say Fikret Abdic, but then Dudakovic managed to defeat Fikret Abdic's forces and he locked around 72.000 civilians who were followers of Fikret Abdic's army in a camp and defeated his army numbering some 15.000 men. He must have been encouraged by this so he took a unit of the corps numbering 25.000 men who had cutting-edge technology, including rifles that weren't even in possession of Pentagon. In the span of seven days he occupied, devastated, plundered, 250 square kilometres of Serb-held territory out of an area called --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means that the 1993 UNPROFOR report was a false report. Under 2, in the span of a year or a year and a half, weapons reached the safe area of Bihac. This means that somebody violated the embargo that the Security Council imposed in one of its resolutions prohibiting the shipments of weapons and ammunition into Western Bosnia. I think that my answer went beyond your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Earlier you said: "In the span of seven days he occupied, devastated, plundered 250 square kilometres of Serb-held territory out of an area called," and what did you then say? The name you referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The area of Grmec, Mount Grmec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that what you said here was from the safe area. That's what the Judge asked you. Is that what you said, 250 kilometres of Serb-held territory from the area that was called?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, and I underlined, from the Bihac safe area, where there were not supposed to be any armed persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did UNPROFOR react to this wide-ranging offensive from the Bihac area?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In no way whatsoever. They simply did not do or say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have any specific examples, or is this just your general knowledge, in relation to the growth of the 5th Corps in Bihac and its arming?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just had two facts that any lay person could compare. I had a report from UNPROFOR from 1993, to the effect that the 5th Corps had been disarmed, all three brigades. Also, I had the fact that I clashed with a corps of 2 -- of 22.000 persons. I don't think that nothing should be added to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question? You referred to disarmament of the -- I think from Bihac under Article 60 of Protocol I, Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions. Now, you earlier told us that two safe areas were established on the basis of an agreement, whereas the others were imposed by the Security Council. You added that Mouth Igman was the third one where an agreement was reached later on as well. Article 60 of Protocol I seems to me to deal mainly with agreed safe areas, not imposed safe areas. Could you explain -- and the Chamber has looked, I think, earlier at the underlying documents for Bihac -- could you explain why you think that Article 60 of Protocol I would apply here, if there is no agreement? And, Mr. Lukic, if we come to this, I have stressed that again and again, if we are talking about this kind of instruments, we should look at the text of those instruments and then analyse them carefully rather than making loose references to it. Could you explain why you think that, where you said it was imposed and not agreed, why Article 60 would nevertheless apply? If you don't know, please tell us, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I can just give my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These weapons, could they have entered the area of Bihac without the participation of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was impossible without UNPROFOR knowing about it. As for participation, I cannot claim anything, whether they did participate or not, but it was impossible for UNPROFOR not to know about convoys of weapons passing through.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: UNPROFOR stated beforehand that Bihac had been declared a safe area. How did the Army of Republika Srpska react then?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We just took note of it because we did not have the right to ask for a joint commission that would verify the extent of disarmament because agreements had not been signed. Again, I am going back to the fact that this was declared in a unilateral way by the Security Council, and had UNPROFOR abided by Article 60 as referred to by the Presiding Judge, had they not actually applied that, they would not have informed us that the corps had been disarmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the same -- why would UNPROFOR have to abide by Article 60 of the 1st protocol? I mean, it's a good analysis of the legal situation, legal instruments, okay. But then, please, on the basis of proper approach, that means texts, analysis of texts, and clear questions and not sweeping statements. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I'm not asking you to interpret legal documents for us. Rather, I believe that you are telling us about what your experience was in the field; right? Who informed you about that, namely that Bihac had been declared a safe area, and who was informed?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff was informed by our Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know -- all right. I'll leave that for now. After the action taken by the 5th Corps from the Bihac safe area, when this corps covered 250 square kilometres of territory that was previously held by the Army of Republika Srpska, did the Army of Republika Srpska at a particular point in time launch a counter-offensive?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska, in the period from the 30th of October until the 3rd of November, stopped the offensive of the Muslim army, and on the 4th of November they launched a counterattack. Over the next 16 days, they returned the territories lost, regained them, and then, until Jimmy Carter arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was typical trench warfare in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is time for our break now so we will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before we take the break, Mr. Lukic, when I commented on sweeping statements, I said Mr. Lukic. But perhaps it would have been better in view of the question you put to the witness, to directly address the witness because your question did not solicit any sweeping statements or any such thing. I would like to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should have phrased it differently. The witness may follow the usher. We take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to deal with a few procedural matters, and for the first one I'd like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to briefly deal with a translation issue which was related to document D290. On the 20th of May of this year, document D290 was admitted into evidence with Witness Mirko Trivic. On the same day, related to D290, a translation issue was raised by the Defence. The question raised was whether, and I quote, "Keep them under guard," is the accurate translation of the original, and the Chamber would like the Defence to inform it whether it submitted a verification request and if there is any follow-up information on this issue. I can imagine that you could not immediately answer, Mr. Lukic, but could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We did ask for a checkup from CLSS and still I'm not satisfied with the translation we received. So, somehow this has to be solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, CLSS considers it an accurate translation but you still want to challenge that. Then we'll further hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, sorry, I just consulted with our Case Manager. That's why he's here. And still I didn't know the full information so we will have to check with them and I'll get back to you, Your Honours, again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do understand you well that the first result of the request for verification is that the translation is accurate but you are still not -- you still want to challenge that by whatever means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's hereby on the record. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the matter raised in private session, the Chamber is correct, I think the matter of confusion was that the tendering of the exhibit was done at a date different than the date that the witness testified so there is no need to check. We understand exactly what the Chamber wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No need to check. I have to praise Chamber's staff for its accuracy. Then before the witness enters the courtroom and perhaps halfway I might invite the usher to already escort the witness into the courtroom but I would like to deliver an oral decision. The Chamber delivers its oral decision on the Prosecution's motion for leave to amend its Rule 65 ter witness list to add Witness RM184. On the 23rd of August, the Prosecution filed a confidential motion seeking leave to add Witness RM184 to its Rule 65 ter witness list as a proposed Rule 92 bis witness. The Prosecution submits that this addition should be considered in light of its 20th of June, 2013, notice of its intention to reduce the evidence it adduces in support of its case. The Prosecution submits that given the decrease in the number of viva voce witnesses, and of the number of witnesses overall, resulting from the notice and the motion, the Defence will require less preparation time for the remaining Prosecution witnesses and will not be prejudiced, which constitutes good cause for the addition and demonstrates that it is in the interests of justice. Further, the Prosecution submits that the proposed additional evidence is needed due to recent developments in the case law of the Tribunal and to practical difficulties in locating the witness. The Prosecution submits that even if it lacks good cause, the witness's evidence is relevant and of probative value and it's in the interests of justice to grant the proposed addition. On the 6th of September, the Defence filed its response, objecting to the motion in its entirety on grounds that the Prosecution has failed to establish good cause for the late addition of the witness and that the addition would prejudice the accused's right to a fair trial. The Defence further objects to the motion based on the proposed mode of testimony. The Chamber recalls and refers to the applicable law concerning amendments to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter witness list as set out in its previous decision filed on the 22nd of August, 2013. The Chamber firstly notes, as it has done in the past, that the Defence's objection regarding the mode of testimony through which Witness RM184 is proposed to testify are premature and misplaced. The proper forum for such objections is in response to a motion tendering the evidence, not a motion for an addition to the 65 ter list. The Chamber will thus not consider arguments concerning the proposed mode of testimony. The Chamber considers that the witness's evidence, which relates to the shelling of Sarajevo, is prima facie relevant and of probative value and may therefore be of assistance to the Chamber in its adjudication of the case. Considering further the difficulty experienced by the Prosecution in locating the witness, the Chamber finds that the Prosecution has demonstrated good cause for the late addition of this witness to its Rule 65 ter witness list. Taking into account the Prosecution's intention to tender Witness RM184's evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis, and the possibility of granting additional time to the Defence to respond to the Rule 92 bis motion, should it so require, along with the Prosecution's submission that it disclosed to the Defence the material related to Witness RM184 on the 16th of August of this year, the Chamber finds that the late addition of the witness does not place an undue burden on the Defence. The Chamber therefore finds that it is in the interests of justice to allow the addition of Witness RM184 to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter witness list and grants the motion. This concludes the Chamber's decision. Meanwhile, the witness may be escorted into the courtroom. I think the usher is already on his way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, we were on the topic of Bihac before the break. The forces of NATO, did they bomb you on the 21st, 22nd and 23rd of November that year? Also, at that moment, were you advancing or were you standing in place, if you will? I'm referring to the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did strike at the time that you referred to, and before that I had a few warnings from General Rose. We had almost regained the territory lost and we were fighting above Bihac on this mountain, and right now the name escapes me. Right above the hospital in Bihac. I even remember the trig, 633. Rose called me and told me to stop or he would strike. And I asked him, Where should I stop? And he said, Stop at the border of the safe area. However, the safe areas of Bihac, Tuzla and Sarajevo were not delimited. They had just been declared. I said that, I don't know where the border is because there isn't one. That conversation took place sometime on the 20th of November. He said to me that I would get a letter of intentions from him. I didn't know what that meant. That is a political document, and we are generals. Anyway, I did not stop. However, I received fire, or rather our intelligence people had already told me that probably on the next day there would be a strike, and the strike did take place in the afternoon, sometime after 1400 hours. During the night before the strike, I applied a regulation. I got my infantry as close as possible to the Muslim infantry because I knew that if he were to hit me, the Muslims could not remain unaffected, and I knew that he could not hit the Muslims. Anyway, there was fire on the 21st, 22nd and 23rd of November. I still hadn't received that letter of intent and I would like to speak about that once you put that question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off and could the general please be asked to speak closer to the microphone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to come a bit closer to the microphone? The interpreters have difficulties in hearing you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, when were you informed about the borders of the Bihac safe area? Before the bombing, after the bombing, when?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The day after the bombing, on the 24th of November, sometime in the evening, that's when I got this letter of intent. Actually it was no letter of intent. There was no text in there. It was just the border of the safe area of Bihac. It exactly coincided with the front of the Serb forces. That is to say that I had not infringed upon the safe area but I was not supposed to go any further. I was not bothered by that very much because the mission had been accomplished. The territory that had been taken away from us had been regained. It is interesting, this map on which I received the borders. The map was signed on the morning of the 24th, and I received it in the evening, about 2000 hours. Now, how it arrived from New York during that period of time or whether it was done in Sarajevo, that is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that your unit that was hit by NATO had not actually infringed upon the borders of the Bihac safe area as defined by the letter that you received, the letter of intent?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to that map, I had not infringed upon the safe area border.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now something else about the bringing in of weapons into the safe areas. Did you know that international humanitarian organisations violated the embargo and brought weapons to the Muslim forces there?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who was it who brought weapons into the enclaves? I don't know. But it -- the weapons did arrive. In the month of January 1994, we analysed the combat readiness of the Drina Corps, and I learned there that when it came to the three safe areas, Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde, there were 16.500 armed men grouped into two divisions and an independent brigade. The 28th Division was in Srebrenica, in the town of Srebrenica, that is. It had about 6500 troops. In the Gorazde safe area, the 81st Muslim division was deployed and it had about 7500 men. In Zepa, there was an independent brigade with about 1200 men in it. For both me and the Main Staff, as well as for the Army of Republika Srpska, that was proof that weapons did manage to enter the safe areas. Second of all, armed people entered the safe areas, soldiers. Before we learned about the numerical strength of those units, there were several incursions out of Srebrenica and attacks on the surrounding villages, and all that was aimed at plundering and getting food supplies. Sometime in mid-March 1994, a lieutenant-colonel called Sejdic [phoen] left Gorazde together with a unit with 750 men. He plundered the Serbian villages on Semic [phoen] mountain which is between Rogatica and Visegrad. Our forces forced him to return to the safe area. This means that while he was exiting the safe area, he had to pass through the UNPROFOR check-points or encirclement, and the same was true when he went back. In Srebrenica the same things happened. They would break out of Srebrenica during the night. If there was opposition on the Serb side, people would be killed and then they would return into Srebrenica in the morning. This compelled us to step up control of humanitarian convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll come to humanitarian convoys and the controls that were stepped up but I would like to speak in more general terms about protected areas or, rather, safe areas. In those areas, it is a fact and it is beyond dispute in this trial that military installations and military units were mixed with the civilian population. Do you know that the Muslim side was offered to demilitarise, for example, for Sarajevo to be demilitarised? Do you know anything about those offers, negotiations? Who was it who offered things? Who was it who didn't want to accept them?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew from public appearances and from personal exchanges that on several occasions President Karadzic insisted on cease-fire and that Sarajevo was divided, or the other way around. First, Sarajevo was to be divided and then there would be cease-fire in Sarajevo which would be proclaimed an open city or an undefended city. According to that system, there would be no armed men and no fire would be opened in the city. As far as I know, the Muslim side always found some excuses or pretexts why not to do it. There were provocations from mortars which were mounted on vehicles. For example, a vehicle would stop at a crossroads, it would fire a few shells, and then it would hastily leave the area and that would provoke Serbian observers to open fire on the place where the fire had been opened from. However, before that, the vehicle would have already been gone, so it would appear as if the Serbs were the one who were opening uncontrolled or indiscriminate or non-selective fire, that we were talking about yesterday. I know that the last offer that was tabled -- or, rather, it was President Karadzic's intervention, was on the eve of the signing of the agreement of the withdrawal of weapons from Sarajevo, the artillery that is. Karadzic offered the United Nations to have Sarajevo proclaimed an open city.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, is it true that the Muslim side did not accept that proposal?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never accepted it. I am aware of a situation, there were negotiations either in Geneva or London, I don't know where, it was a conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a matter of fact. Haris Silajdzic did not want to attend that session. He didn't want to listen to Karadzic talking about reconciliation or a cease-fire. While he was talking about that, Haris Silajdzic actually walked out of the room and left the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let me ask you about something about Srebrenica. Is it true that the entire life in Srebrenica was militarised? Whatever social fabric existed, it was actually controlled by the 28th Division and that included the distribution of humanitarian aid and other such things?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear that from anybody. However, I could actually experience it. I realised that Naser Oric had all the power in his hands, humanitarian convoys, military authorities, civilian authorities. When humanitarian convoys arrived it was the military that distributed aid and not some other neutral organisation like the Red Cross or some other such civilian body. I must tell you one more thing. I've already shared with you the contents of my conversations with General Philippe Morillon as regards the number of refugees in these places. He said that there were 64.000 refugees in Srebrenica, and UNHCR had that figure in mind when planning their humanitarian aid. However, we knew that there were 42.000 refugees tops in Srebrenica, not more than that, which means that there was a surplus of food, clothing, footwear and other things, for 20.000 more people than actually were recorded in Srebrenica. And all that was for the purpose of the army. The same thing was in Zepa. The official data spoke about 32.000, whereas we were only aware of some 18.000 refugees actually residing in Zepa. So there was a discrepancy in these figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us what period you are referring to? According to some Muslim documents before the fall of Srebrenica, there were about 36 [as interpreted] inhabitants residing in Srebrenica. Are you talking about a period preceding the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period between January and March 1993, before the enclave fell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it correct what I see in the transcript, that in your question you were referring to "36 inhabitants residing in Srebrenica"?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to the Muslim documents and it's part of our evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you something else about UNPROFOR. Did it happen that UNPROFOR soldiers also acted as a human shield for Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that for a fact. However, they did collaborate. They were their forward defence detachment as it were. For example, UNPROFOR helicopter were used to transport the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina, i.e., Alija Izetbegovic, to Srebrenica, or the Srebrenica authorities to various meetings which took place either in Sarajevo and Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I meant to ask you actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I again revisit the issue of the inhabitants where you said it is according to the Muslim documents. The number was 36, not 36.000? Just 36 persons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what Judge Fluegge was seeking to clarify but 36.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe I misspoke. A bit more than 36.000 actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we are back on track. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is it true that General Morillon, in February 1993, with 19 of his soldiers, protected Muslims by actually having mingled with them, if you are at all aware of that situation?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am well aware of that situation because our commander, General Mladic, authorised me to be in charge of the negotiations with Morillon and so on and so forth. That happened in February and March. Sometime at the beginning of March, I believe that it was around the 9th or 10th of March, General Morillon took 19 of his soldiers, who were his protection detail, and entered Srebrenica. I thought that it was his regular activity, i.e., touring safe areas. However, General Morillon did not leave Srebrenica for the next few days. I believe that General Morillon was kept there by force, I don't want to use the word "kidnapped," so as to have the UNPROFOR unit in the centre of Srebrenica which deprived us of our legitimate right to pound the Muslim army in Srebrenica. General Mladic and President Karadzic did not really believe my assessment. They thought that Morillon stayed there of his own will. However, on the 13th of March, I received an invitation from Morillon to meet him in Bratunac on the following day, on the 14th. Obviously I sought approval from General Mladic. The general told me, Go and see what he wants. I arrived in Bratunac on the following day. We were supposed to meet at 1600 hours. A message or a courier arrived. I don't know how the message actually arrived at the brigade command where I was waiting for Morillon. According to that message, Morillon could not come to Bratunac but, rather, he requested me to come to a feature called Zuta Zemlja which is some about halfway between Bratunac and Srebrenica. General Tolimir was also a member of my delegation as well as Colonel Rajko Balac. At first, Tolimir tried to persuade me not to go. However, the final decision was reached and we went. We arrived there and we found Morillon in a garage. There was a house nearby. And Colonel Balac observed the situation around that house and he realised that the surrounding elevations were taken by Muslim soldiers. He asked my approval to prepare artillery support while Morillon and I were talking. Obviously I gave him my approval but he was not supposed to open fire without my order. Morillon gave me the impression that he had been kept by force. The general is very pedantic normally but I saw him not very clean shaven. His nails were dirty. He asked me for a cigarette. I know that he was smoking some very thin cigarettes and that he rolled his own. I gave him a pack of cigarettes. We talked and then I asked him, General, are you being kept here by force or not? And the general said, No, no, no I'm just doing my job. He told me that on the following day he would leave Srebrenica to prove that he had not been kept by force. We kept on talking about the same topic that we discussed back in January and that was the withdrawal of the sick and wounded from Srebrenica. At that moment I didn't mention Tuzla at all because I knew that it would have been in vain. We were engaged in a lengthy conversation about Srebrenica. Look, that was on the 14th of March, and our forces had taken Cerska, Kamenica, and we had reached as far as Konjevic Polje. On the southern side or the south-eastern side, we came close to Guber Banja which is some two kilometres away from Srebrenica. There had already been a lot of talks about that in the Main Staff. I accepted that but I did not take any decisions. I told him that I would inform General Mladic and I would suggest that we should accept his proposal because our forces would be free as a result of that. That's how our conversation ended, and on the following day, Morillon left Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now Bihac briefly, please. Were you able to observe Muslim troops acting behind UN APCs in the Bihac area?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But from the trig point 633, I was able to observe, in the compound of the Bihac hospital, 11 APCs belonging to the UN because they had a flag hoisted on the central APC, lined up. And I wasn't even able to contemplate any strikes or fire upon the area surrounding the hospital compound because I would be hitting the UN. It was on the 22nd or the 23rd of December that I was at this trig point for the last time, so it was a month later, roughly, and the APCs were still parked there although by that time we already had the so-called Carter truce in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you about the agreement where you took part, involving UNPROFOR participants. You mentioned it today. It's the agreement to demilitarise Igman and Bjelasnica, the two mounts. You did participate in the negotiations for the agreement, right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Mladic and Karadzic were attending one of the peace conferences in Geneva, I believe. It was on the 11th or 12th of August, in the morning, that I spoke to President Karadzic. He told me that I had to withdraw the Serbian forces from Mounts Igman and Bjelasnica. I was asking to be put through to General Mladic in order to receive that order from him. General Mladic gave a categorical "no" and thus I found myself between a rock and a hard stone, where the Supreme Commander ordered that I should withdraw and my military commander that I should not. I asked Karadzic that the two of them come to an agreement and get back to me later on what I was supposed to be doing because the withdrawal of the troops from mounts Igman and Bjelasnica, that we had been advancing towards for the past four months, constituted a very risky step for the commanding officer. We were in touch again on the following morning. General Mladic was a bit more flexible. He told me that I should do the best I can but that I should not hand the territory over to the Muslims. But all right, that was already a glimmer of hope, that I had a way out of the situation. We met on the 12th of August, the British general, David Hayes, the chief of UNPROFOR staff for the BH, and I. We spoke the whole morning but were not able to find a way of withdrawing the Serb army without allowing the Muslims to occupy mounts Igman and Bjelasnica. That day ended without an agreement having been reached. Nobody from the Muslim Supreme Command attended these negotiations. We agreed that we would resume talks on the following day, in that same place. I set off for Trnovo. On the way, I received a call over the radio from President Karadzic. The conversation began with some terrible shouting. I do believe the Tribunal has a recording of it: Why didn't you withdraw? You have to withdraw. There was a lot of shouting involved. I asked to be put through to Mladic again. However, the line between Karadzic and me broke off. I thought that Karadzic was the one who rang off so as to prevent me from speaking to Mladic. Hayes and I met in that same place and Hayes told me I would not like to be in your shoes, general. How will you pull back the army that you kept pushing forward from Visegrad towards Igman for several months? But, he said, I have a proposal to make, should I accept it. Now, his proposal was that the UNPROFOR forces would take positions along ten points on Igman and Bjelasnica, and would thus take control of these areas. We would withdraw the army and they would prevent the Muslims from occupying Igman and Bjelasnica. This was some sort of way out. We agreed, and we were supposed to go to Mount Igman to determine precisely what the separation line would be. I found the commander of Sarajevo Corps in -- stationed in Famos Hotel. However, instead of reporting to me, upon seeing me, he attacked me, where have you been so far? Mladic and Karadzic were looking for you. I was on the line again with Karadzic. He started shouting and I said, President, we agreed, and this will be implemented. He required that it be implemented by 1600 hours of that same day. We drafted the agreement there and then. Hayes and I signed it. I went back to Crna Rijeka. Hayes told me he would send me two copies of the agreement once the Muslim side had signed it. He gave me a call in the evening and told me that Rasim Delic refused to sign the agreement. Instead he was offering somebody else of your same rank to sign it. That's to say the Chief of Staff. And I said, Fine, let Sifer sign it. And that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we are six minutes away from the time of the next break. Could we expect another question to the witness or is it just that he freely tells and whatever comes to his mind seems to be relevant or important for us to know? Is that your position? Then examination of witness, I do understand, to be slightly different from what happens at this moment. Mr. Mladic wants to consult with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic should remain seated and speak at low volume. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the practice before this Tribunal is somewhat different. We are expected to put questions to you more often, and, well, the way you went on talking you've actually covered eight pages of my questions. That's why I've been letting you expand the story a bit further because it seems that we proceed faster that way. Sifer is the Chief of Staff of the BH Army; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Deputy Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their Chief of Staff was also the Commander-in-Chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I found Sifer in your statements but would it possibly have been Siber?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Siber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The guarantor of the agreement was Hayes; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is what interests me the most. What was the role that General Hayes assumed between the BH Army and the VRS with respect to this agreement?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR assumed the role of guarantor, that the Muslims would not be taking up the mounts of Igman and Bjelasnica once we left. Hayes said that following this agreement between the two of us, Rasim Delic added three more points because we agreed on ten points, and Rasim Delic added three more points and thus UNPROFOR took up 13 positions in all from which they were able to have under their control what was formerly our forward defence positions. So that was the role that he assumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did General Hayes sign the agreement, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Hayes signed it. And on the following day, the 14th, Generals Hayes and Brinkman, UNPROFOR commander, handed the agreement to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because of some of the discussions we had earlier on, I want to ask you this: With his signature on the document, would General Hayes be taking upon himself some of the obligations? Was this your understanding of the situation? And was this General Hayes's understanding of the situation?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The agreement was that once he would take positions on all the 13 points, I would start with the retreat of the Serbian army. And that's how it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, as you sit here today, the names of these various points that UNPROFOR occupied?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did give a statement to that effect. It was Bijelo Brdo, Tresnjevo Brdo, the hills there, but I can't really enumerate them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we are talking already for quite a while about texts and signatures. Could you assist me. Is this in evidence? And, if so, under what numbers so that we are better able to follow the testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will try to locate it during the break which is in five minutes, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in five minutes, just as you -- I think we resumed at ten minutes to 11.00. Five more minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] UNPROFOR took positions on the 13 points and the VRS handed them over. What happened next? What happened over the course of the next 13 months, say?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire process was done in a month. UNPROFOR took positions and the VRS units, that is to say the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, withdrew the VRS troops. As the troops left the last point occupied by UNPROFOR, a Muslim unit appeared out of nowhere and literally slaughtered, cut the throats of 37 Serb soldiers and wounded 34 of them. I lodged a protest with General Rose, UNPROFOR commander, accompanied with threats. I don't know what he did in response to that. In the next three months, the Muslims captured these various points from UNPROFOR, one by one, and I think that before the new years' eve they had Igman and Bjelasnica under their control. I know that General Hayes left his post before the end of his term because UNPROFOR did not honour that particular item of the agreement to protect Igman and Bjelasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm leaving this area so it may be a good time for a break and we will try to locate that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We take a break of 20 minutes. Mr. Milovanovic, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to move into private session for a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. For the public record, the Chamber has, through an oral decision, admitted 18 documents into evidence under seal when we were in private session. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, my mistake, but now thanks to the insistence of the Trial Chamber, we are going to take a look at the agreement that we discussed. We need P25 in e-court. The document has four pages in the English version because there is a preceding UNPROFOR report. We see that Brigadier Hayes authorised the sending or the release of this document. Now we are going to move on to the first page and now, actually, could we look at the third page, please? We will see the map there. The points are marked on that map. This is a copy that has been a bit cut off. So we see Major General Manojlo and then down there, we see Brigadier Veer Hayes. And now page 4 in both languages, could we see that? Can we see what it was that was agreed upon? Now, this is what it says here. A -- military commanders agreed on the following. The undersigned military commanders of representatives of the parties in the conflict have agreed on the following, and then it says Article 1, the line of confrontation. The line of confrontation as it existed on the 30th of July, 1993, and then there is something handwritten that was added and that was signed by UNPROFOR. As defined by UNPROFOR is the line marked on the attached map. Article 2, withdrawal of the forces that were momentarily - at that moment, that is to say - under the command of Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic. It says that forces would withdraw to the east by the 14th of August, 1993, at 1600 hours. Article 3 envisaged the consolidation of the forces momentarily under command of General Rasim Delic. And it says the forces momentary under command of General Rasim Delic within the area as marked on the map will not move from their locations to fill the area vacated by the Serbian forces. We see the signatures here. We see that this was signed by Mr. Stjepan Siber, Major-General Manojlo Milovanovic, witnessed by Brigadier Veer Hayes. At the top of the page, we can see that it is an agreement for withdrawal of forces from Igman and Bjelasnica. General, is this the agreement that you testified about before we took the break?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the Trial Chamber has some additional questions for the witness. Otherwise I'm done with the topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to the extent that what brings it -- what we did not know already. That would be my only question. I mean it is in evidence. We heard the evidence not only about the agreement but also about how it was violated, when and where and by whom. So, therefore, I wondered what news we've learned in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to abide by your -- Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I see that we wanted to have a look at the document itself because you were putting all kinds of questions to the witness without even having the text available, but then the same question remains: What do we know more now apart from that the witness participated in the preparation of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, now we know the personal insight of this witness, who was part of this agreement, and who was part of a later developments that were in a contradiction with the agreement. And we have first-hand insight. We only through this witness we were able to have the first-hand insight in this incident or the whole series of incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's what you say. That's what you tell us. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, now I'd like to move on to a different topic. The topic will be the situation during the war and command. I won't have many questions. However, what I would like to confirm with you that the war was not declared at the very beginning of the war operations. You already mentioned that, albeit indirectly.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The state of war was not declared in Republika Srpska. It was just an immediate threat of war that was declared. Peacetime acts and laws were still in effect and applied to defence. During the war, on two occasions in parts of the territory of Republika Srpska, the state of war was indeed declared and that was the first time in November 1994, due to the situation surrounding Bihac that we already discussed. That was to enable us to prevent desertion from the army. The second time it happened during the Muslim offensive to de-block Sarajevo. That's what they called the operation. And that operation lasted from the 16th to the 25th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You arrived in B and H after April. However, did you learn subsequently, in the course of your work, what was proclaimed on the 4th of April, 1992, by Alija Izetbegovic? Was that an immediate threat of war? I'm talking about 4th of April then, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 4th of April, Alija Izetbegovic declared an immediate threat of war and he issued a communique about the general mobilisation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the 6th of April, the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised. On the 4th of August, 1992, the Muslim authorities declared a state of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you about Srebrenica, about the critical time in Srebrenica. You were already asked about that but I believe that the questions were rather hypothetical. Today, I would like to show you a piece of evidence in this case. Dragan Obrenovic, the Chief of Staff and the deputy commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we move to private session for a short?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like call up P1469.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Directive 7, with your accompanying letter, you've already spoken about this in many details. My question is whether you would agree with me that the process of the Supreme Command issuing orders to corps is actually skipping a step in the chain of command, i.e., by-passing the Main Staff, which should be in the middle between the two.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General Miletic received all the guidelines to draft this directive from the Supreme Commander; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would it also be true that he couldn't, and I'm referring to General Miletic, or, rather, that he didn't have to consult the assistance of the Main Staff commander because he had already received all the guidelines that enabled him to draft the directive from the Supreme Commander; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't have to. However, if I'd been in his shoes, I would have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now on to directive 7/1. That's the following document, P1470.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, could I ask you the following: You were asked whether General Miletic receives all the guidelines to draft this directive from the Supreme Commander. You said yes. What is the basis of this knowledge? What do you know about what Miletic received from Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that when I was testifying between the 29th of May and 1st of June, from General Miletic's Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the real answer to the question is: I do not know. I heard someone who is Defence counsel for Mr. Miletic to take a certain position, and that's -- so you don't have any actual knowledge about it, from whom he received guidelines in drafting that directive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I pushed things too far. I came across this information in the transcript. However, I thought that you might know that directive 7, because you've already testified to that effect -- or, rather, that directive 7/1 amended directive 7, primarily when it comes to the tasks to be given to the Drina Corps; namely directive 7/1 does not contain Operation Krivaja 95; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that directive 7/1, which I'm sure you've read on a number of occasions, as well as the other one, does not reference directive 7 anywhere. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say "as well as the other one." Which other one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually my question should be: Is it also true that directive 7/1, which I'm sure you've read on a number of occasions, does not reference directive 7 anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, directive 7/1 was supposed to commence like this. Pursuant to directive 7 issued by the Supreme Commander on such and such a date and then the text of the directive would follow. So it should have been mentioned in the first sentence. You are right that in his directive 7/1, General Mladic does not invoke or refer to the directive issued by the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That particular action by the Drina Corps, namely Krivaja 95 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I take you back? Do I understand that the question was whether any reference is made to directive 7 in directive 7/1? Is that -- was that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let me have a look at page 2 in English. I read there, just last line of paragraph 1: "Other details of the intentions and possibilities of enemy forces are in directive number 7 and daily intelligence reports of the VRS Main Staff." So I have some difficulties in understanding that no reference was ever made to directive number 7 in this text after having read it several times, as the witness said, where upon reading it now, not for the first time but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps my question wasn't properly phrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you go to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's the last line of paragraph 1. And then the first line of paragraph 2 starts, "On the basis of directive number 7, the VRS has the task," et cetera. So I'm totally lost with evidence saying that no reference was made in 7/1 to 7. But if you have any further explanation, then -- or any further questions on the matter, I'd be glad to hear such questions and the answers to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, I think we understood each other but I'll reformulate. The Main Staff did not adopt directive 7. Rather, it only took those portions of it that it believed it should. We see that the intentions and capabilities of the enemy are mentioned here, and this is something that can be found in directive 7 as well. However, the tasks assigned to the Drina Corps were not taken over from directive 7; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could draw Mr. Lukic's attention to the third reference on page 3 of the original and page 4 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we get page 3, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can assist further it says, "By carrying out ...," quote: "By carrying out planned combat battles and operations in accordance with directive number 7 ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question had to do with the Drina Corps. The Drina Corps is mentioned only on page 5 of the directive. I wasn't dealing with the east Bosnia corps or the other corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise about the confusion, General. My question added to it. I'll repeat what I said a moment ago: Is it true that the task assigned to the Drina Corps in directive 7/1 was not taken over from directive 7?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Two things were left out in directive 7/1 that can be read in directive 7. The first is this controversial sentence that unbearable conditions be created for the population. And what was also left out is the sentence referring to the separation of Srebrenica and Zepa, or from Zepa, by force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, please clarify for me for better understanding of the document. The reference to directive 7 is found at the beginning of this document, and then we see on the screen, under item 5, tasks of units.
